title: Counting breaths
hookLine: counting out-breaths to ten, the first practice many Zen students learn

lines: WAIT, WHAT NUMBER WAS I ON?
cards: And somewhere around there, the shopping list arrives. Then an email that needs answering. Then a scene from last night's show.
Then, with a small jolt: wait, what number was I on? Fourteen? Twenty-two?
It can look like failing at a very simple task. Zen sees it differently: that jolt is where the practice actually happens. The posture is built.

teach.b: Susokukan is Japanese for the contemplation of counting breaths. In Zen it's often given to beginners early on, sometimes on the first day.
The method: sit in this week's posture and let the breath come and go by itself; nothing about it needs to change. On the first out-breath, count one, silently. On the next, two.
Up to ten, then start again at one. That's all.

teach.h: ONE TO TEN, ON THE OUT-BREATH.
teach.b: Some teachers have students count both the in-breath and the out-breath at first, and only the out-breath later. Then the rule that matters.
When the count is lost, or you notice you've sailed past ten, you go back to one. No scolding, no starting the sit over. Just one.
In this practice the return is not a detour from the work; it is the work. Someone who loses count fifty times in a sit hasn't failed fifty times. They've come back fifty times.
Counting the breath is older than Zen.

teach.h: A FIRST STEP, MEANT TO BE PUT DOWN.
teach.b: Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification, a classic manual of the Theravada tradition, describes counting as a first step in mindfulness of breathing, a way to tie a wandering mind to something simple.
And it is meant to be put down. When the count steadies, teachers may have students drop it and follow the breath without numbers, and later sit with no method at all. Tomorrow, that last step.

how: In Zen centers, beginners are often taught to count out-breaths from one to ten, returning to one whenever they lose count, before moving to following the breath or to just sitting.

o: breathing in a slow, set rhythm
holding the breath to calm the mind
counting out-breaths from one to ten

s: losing count means the sit has failed
going back to one is the practice itself.
in susokukan you count the out-breaths from one to ten
counting breaths means breathing in a special rhythm
the breath goes at its own pace; only the count is added.

games.q: you're counting breaths and suddenly notice you're on twenty-three. what do you do?
games.why: back to one, without scolding. the return is the practice.

practice: In your posture, with the breath going at its own pace, count one silently on the next out-breath, two on the next, up to ten, then begin again at one.
When a thought carries you off and you notice, don't argue with it; just come back to one. Reaching ten is fine, and never getting past three is fine too.

wordCard.voice: Susokukan. Japanese for counting breaths: one to ten on the out-breath, and back to one whenever the count is lost. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: the contemplation of counting breaths.

carryVoice: Your line: one to ten. However often the count slips, one is always there to come back to. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga VIII (counting as the first stage of mindfulness of breathing)
